quote: Nobody calls from the school and nobody says one thing to her all day.
why: reports an absent reaction/event as proof the day is unremarkable instead of showing the day's texture
suggestion: The phone doesn't ring. Nobody stops at her desk. She sits behind the same sheet with different numbers on it.

quote: where nobody minds her being and nobody talks to her either
why: uses two absent reactions to stand in as evidence of her isolation rather than a specific physical detail
suggestion: where the other kids' backs stay turned and the seat next to her stays empty

quote: which gets her most of the way to the bell
why: a trailing which-clause that tells the reader how to take the coloring detail (that it's killing time) instead of letting the image stand
suggestion: Cut it: "...going right up to the lines without going over them anywhere."

quote: She's just sitting there in the gap with her coat still on.
why: "just" softens a claim the narrator is entitled to make plainly about what Chloe is doing
suggestion: She's sitting there in the gap with her coat still on.

quote: She says she'll be good, and that she'll do the dishes
why: "She says" is repeated seven times as the frame verb across this paragraph, the exact pattern the guide names as an automatic fail
suggestion: Drop the frame verb after the first use: "She says she'll be good, do the dishes every night for the rest of her life. Her dad's jobs too, all of them, without being asked..."

quote: It's the only whole sentence she manages
why: narrator superlative ("only") ranking the sentence rather than describing it; the rule allows superlatives in dialogue but bans them in narration
suggestion: It's a whole sentence, and she gets it out twice.

quote: it isn't school and it isn't the sheets and it isn't Kayleigh Burns
why: three repeated "it isn't X" beats chained in one sentence, the anaphora pattern the guide says to collapse
suggestion: Chloe can't answer that one; school, the sheets, Kayleigh Burns, none of them alone is it.

quote: It's all three of those and it's none of them
why: the two clauses are grammatically mirrored (It's X / it's Y), the exact symmetric-halves construction the guide bans in narration
suggestion: It's some of each, and she is seven years old with no word for any of it.

quote: she can hear him not making dinner
why: routes the stimulus through the perception verb "hear" instead of rendering the absence of kitchen sound directly
suggestion: and from the floor, no pans, no water, just her dad's feet on the kitchen tile, going nowhere

quote: for a second
why: "for a second" is used as a generic duration marker regardless of what's being timed, and recurs at lines 107 and 139
suggestion: somebody runs the tap three, four seconds and turns it off again

quote: Nobody says anything for a while after that.
why: reports an absent reaction to convey the weight of the moment instead of a specific physical detail
suggestion: The fridge hums. Chloe lies with her hands under the pillow, listening to it.

quote: for a while
why: generic duration marker used as a universal timer regardless of the moment, part of a recurring crutch across the chapter
suggestion: replace with a real span or a rendered detail: "Chloe lies with her eyes open, and it's minutes before either of them speaks again."

quote: and nobody says one word to her about any of it
why: reports an absent reaction across weeks as proof of the silence rather than showing a concrete instance of it
suggestion: and at dinner the subject just doesn't come up, night after night

quote: which is how she knows before anybody has said a word about it
why: nearly identical to the guide's own banned example ("...which is how Chloe knows the answer is a real one"); it explains what the preceding image already conveyed
suggestion: Cut it and let the staging do the work: "They sit her down in the living room, both of them at once, on the couch across from her."

quote: what happens next is that we—
why: the style guide bans the em dash outright, however it's typed, with no stated exception for interrupted dialogue
suggestion: "If they say yes, then what happens next is that we..." Chloe is on her feet before he finishes.

quote: Say the whole thing again.
why: "the whole thing" is a named crutch phrase in the style guide and recurs again at line 95
suggestion: "Say it again," Chloe says, still standing. "Say all of it again."

quote: we don't have any way to—
why: second em dash in the chapter; the construction is banned regardless of typing or intended use
suggestion: "Honey, we don't have any way to call her tonight."

quote: quiet enough that Chloe nearly doesn't get it
why: loads the dialogue tag with an explanation of tone/circumstance instead of letting a split action beat carry it
suggestion: Her mom's voice drops. "I know what she's like." Chloe almost misses it through the floor.

quote: not really listening to any of it
why: "really" hedges a claim the close-POV narrator can state plainly, since Chloe herself would know whether she's listening
suggestion: with Chloe on the rug in front of the television, not listening to any of it

quote: on the whole thing
why: second instance of the named crutch phrase "the whole thing" in this chapter (also line 65)
suggestion: "and that's the only condition on the deal."

quote: without putting down what she's holding
why: a prepositional circumstance detail loaded into the dialogue tag rather than split into its own beat
suggestion: Her mother doesn't put down what she's holding. "No. Absolutely not."

quote: Then give me one reason, because I have been sitting here trying to think of one and I can't.
why: this is the fourth consecutive line of dialogue (99-105) with no intervening physical detail anchoring the two speakers in the room
suggestion: Add a beat: "Dave rubs a hand over his face. 'Then give me one reason, because I have been sitting here trying to think of one and I can't.'"

quote: Nobody says anything for a second after that.
why: reports an absent reaction to signal the weight of Meg's speech instead of a physical detail
suggestion: Dave looks at the table. The chair creaks when he shifts his weight.

quote: for a second
why: third use of "for a second" as a generic duration marker in this chapter (also lines 43 and 139)
suggestion: replace with a rendered beat rather than a timed marker, e.g. "Dave looks at the table."

quote: Chloe hears all of that from the rug and understands about a third of it
why: routes the whole exchange through the perception verbs "hears" and "understands" instead of rendering what actually reaches her
suggestion: From the rug, Chloe catches maybe one word in three.

quote: it goes somewhere in her and stays
why: hands the abstract "it" (her partial understanding) a physical verb ("goes," "stays") as though it were an object being stored
suggestion: name what she actually does: "and she doesn't ask what the rest of it meant"

quote: nobody makes anything at all of her being there
why: reports an absent reaction to establish the classroom's ordinariness instead of a concrete detail
suggestion: and the boy next to her just shoves a spare pencil across the table

quote: the part where somebody gives her a test
why: "the part where" is a named crutch phrase, a placeholder standing in for the behavior instead of showing it
suggestion: She keeps waiting for someone to hand her a test, right through the afternoon and out to the car.

quote: The engine is off, the lights are off
why: two grammatically mirrored clauses (X is off, Y is off) in narration, the symmetric-halves construction the guide bans
suggestion: The engine's off and the lights with it, and she hasn't opened her door.

quote: for a second
why: fourth use of "for a second" as a generic duration marker in this chapter
suggestion: Chloe watches her through the window until her dad calls something about toast

quote: Her mother is down on the floor with her by then, in the gap, with both arms round her.
why: the mother's arrival and the comfort she immediately speaks (line 19) are one continuous beat split across two paragraphs
suggestion: Merge with the following line: "Her mother is down on the floor with her by then, in the gap, with both arms round her. 'Baby. Breathe for me. You have to breathe before you can talk.'"

quote: Then say something about it, because I have been the only one saying anything about it since August.
why: fifth consecutive line of dialogue (33-41) with no physical detail anchoring the two speakers at the table
suggestion: Add a beat before it: "She pushes her chair back an inch. 'Then say something about it, because I have been the only one saying anything about it since August.'"

quote: Am I going, though, is it a real thing, are you actually saying yes to it?
why: third consecutive untagged line in an eight-turn exchange (57-71) that relies on the reader counting line breaks to track four speaker turns
suggestion: Chloe grabs the arm of the couch. "Am I going, though, is it a real thing, are you actually saying yes to it?"
